title: Strat Chat - Hinge Questions
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien explains the hinge question as a check for understanding placed after a core concept is taught, offering the correct answer alongside plausible distractors built from common misconceptions. He argues a failed hinge question signals a fault in tier 1 instruction and a need to re-teach before moving on. His preferred format is a carefully crafted multiple-choice item, not one pulled from AI or a textbook. He walks through how each wrong option diagnoses a different gap, so the pattern of student answers tells the teacher whether to re-teach, refine or clarify. He warns against obviously wrong distractors, which turn a hinge question into an early-success check. He notes that experience builds a bank of misconceptions and that AI can help novices if outputs are checked.
points: A hinge question is a post-teaching check whose distractors are plausible misconceptions, so wrong answers reveal exactly what students misunderstand.
If many students choose the misconception options, the author treats it as a signal to re-teach before moving on.
Each distractor should map to a specific error, such as an everyday meaning of a word, or a near-miss answer.
Obviously wrong distractors defeat the purpose and belong in an early confidence-building check instead.
Teachers get better at writing hinge questions as they accumulate knowledge of common misconceptions, and AI drafts need careful vetting.
quotes: In teaching a hinge question is a specific check for understanding after a core concept of the lesson has been taught which presents the students with the correct answer as well as plausible distractions and common misconceptions to allow the teacher to accurately assess understanding before moving on. We refer to this as a hinge because a large proportion of our learning is sequential and builds on what has been learned directly before it and so therefore if the hinge question fails, it shows a fault in tier 1 instruction and a need to adapt or respond before pushing forward.

There are many different ways in which teaching experts suggest that hinge questions can be presented however I believe the best by far is carefully crafted multiple choice question. This is no ordinary multiple choice question you’ve farmed from AI or stolen from a text book. This is a carefully curated question and responses based on common misconceptions and likely student errors.

By carefully curating these questions it provides us as teachers with more useful information than just asking a recall questions or a written response. Not only do we know whether or not the students know. We know what they don’t know. Specifically, the exact misconception that exists that can be explicitly taught against.

In terms of creating a hinge question, it becomes easier the longer you’ve been teaching a particular subject as you will become aware of a larger data-set of all of the common misconceptions that tend to occur in that piece of knowledge. This means that you can learn from the ghosts of the past and use their errors of understanding to inform your future teaching so that our students do not repeat the same mistakes again and more importantly we strengthen the quality of our instruction to maximise the opportunities for our students to succeed.

Teacher beware: there can be a temptation to make the distractor options obviously wrong so our students definitely succeed. This is not a hinge question. This could be performed as a CFU earlier in the lesson so that all students feel success early, however for a hinge question every option should be plausible in some way.

If the majority of students are choosing A or B it sends a signal to the teacher that their instruction was not clear or understood. This would tell the teacher that they need to go back and re-teach that content or use more worked examples before moving on.
I spent too much of my early career teaching assuming students understood and then fuming when they submitted misconceptions in assessments. Check early and check often.
